title: Number Series

steps.title: Look for a repeating rule
steps.content: A number series is generated by a rule. Start by checking consecutive differences. If differences are constant, it is an arithmetic pattern. If not, check second differences, ratios, squares or alternating rules.
steps.tip: Write the differences below the series before guessing.

steps.title: Find the next term
hints: Identify the key concept or constraint in the prompt before looking at the options.
Work through the example one step at a time and eliminate choices that contradict the rule.

steps.title: Recognize multiplication patterns
steps.content: If differences grow quickly, check multiplication or division. A series may also alternate two separate patterns in odd and even positions.
steps.example: 2, 6, 18, 54… multiply by 3 each time, so next = 162.

steps.title: Alternating pattern
steps.explanation: Odd positions: 2,4,6,8. Even positions: 5,7,9. Next is 8.
hints: Identify the key concept or constraint in the prompt before looking at the options.
Work through the example one step at a time and eliminate choices that contradict the rule.

steps.title: Squares and cubes
steps.content: Compare terms with nearby perfect squares or cubes. For example, 1, 8, 27, 64 are 1³, 2³, 3³, 4³.
steps.example: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 are consecutive squares. The next term is 36.

steps.title: Recognize changing differences
steps.explanation: The differences are 3, 5, 7 and 9. The next difference is 11, so 26+11=37.
hints: Subtract each term from the next to reveal the difference sequence.
The differences increase by 2 each time.

steps.title: Solve an alternating series
steps.explanation: Separate odd and even positions. Odd positions are 4, 6, 8, so the next odd-position term is 10. Even positions are 12, 18, 24.
hints: Do not apply one difference to the whole sequence immediately.
Split the terms into odd-position and even-position subsequences.

steps.title: Use a reliable series-solving method
steps.prompt: Arrange the checks you should make when a series is unfamiliar.
options: Test whether the rule fits every given term
Look for alternating positions or familiar powers
steps.explanation: Start with differences and ratios, then test alternating or special-number patterns. Always verify the rule against every term.
hints: Start with the simplest common patterns before inventing a complicated rule.
A candidate rule is not valid until it explains all the supplied terms.

questions.explanation: Differences are 3,5,7,9; next difference is 11, so 27+11=38.

learning_objectives: Validate a proposed rule against every term.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Any two terms are enough to identify the intended rule.
common_misconceptions.correction: Many rules can fit two terms; check the complete sequence and prefer a simple consistent explanation.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Every series uses one constant difference.
common_misconceptions.correction: Some series use ratios, changing differences, alternating subsequences or powers.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A plausible next number is automatically correct.
common_misconceptions.correction: The proposed rule must explain every supplied term, not only the final pair.

worked_examples.title: Use first differences
worked_examples.explanation: A constant first difference identifies an arithmetic progression.

worked_examples.title: Use second differences
worked_examples.explanation: Constant second differences are a useful clue for a quadratic sequence; here the terms are consecutive squares.

worked_examples.title: Split an alternating series
worked_examples.explanation: Interleaved sequences can hide two simple patterns in one list.

company_applications.practice: Write differences and verify a rule across every term.
Test alternating and interleaved patterns systematically.
Explain why a pattern fits all given terms.

srs_cards.question: What should you check first in a number series?
srs_cards.answer: Calculate consecutive differences, then check ratios, alternating positions and familiar powers.

srs_cards.question: What do constant second differences suggest?
srs_cards.answer: A quadratic pattern, often involving square-number behavior.

srs_cards.question: How do you validate a proposed series rule?
srs_cards.answer: Check that it explains every given term, not just the last two.

quest.story: A signal tower sends number sequences with hidden rules. Your team must identify the simplest rule that explains every signal.
quest.mission: Use differences, ratios, alternating subsequences and powers to predict the next term and justify the rule.
success_criteria: Verify a rule against all supplied terms.
